newsitem.title: USA: British Labour Party in no rush to join EMU.
newsitem.headline: British Labour Party in no rush to join EMU.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party signalled on Thursday that it was not in any hurry to jettison the pound sterling and join a single European currency in 1999.

Speaking to reporters following a meeting with U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, Labour economic spokesman Gordon Brown said he saw "real hurdles" that made it "increasingly difficult" for British entry in monetary union in 1999.
"Getting it right is, of course, more important than getting it quickly," he said.
Labour has a substantial lead in opinion polls over the ruling Conservative Party, which is widely expected to call parliamentary elections in May.
Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Wednesday that the government was "on balance hostile" to a single currency, which is scheduled to be launched in 1999.

Finance minister Kenneth Clarke, the most pro-European member of Prime Minister John Major's cabinet, reacted to this apparent breach of the government's agreed "wait and see" line by saying Rifkind must have made a slip of the tongue.

Many Conservatives believe their party's only chance of snatching an election victory would be for them to come out against a single currency and mount a patriotic defence of the pound as a symbol of Britain's sovereignty.
Brown accused the Conservatives of being inconsistent on European monetary union and said Labour would base its decision on entry on a "hard-headed assessment" of what was in the national interest.
"If the economic conditions are right, we will retain the option of joining the single currency in the next parliament and in the first wave," Brown said.
Brown said any decision about British membership should take into account not just the economic criteria laid down in the European Union's Maastricht Treaty, but "our own British economic tests."

Those tests would look at the effect of EMU entry on investment, jobs and the financial services industry in Britain, and would also consider whether EU countries were at different stages of the economic cycle and had enough flexibility to deal with economic problems.
Brown repeated Labour's pledge to submit any proposal to join a single currency to a national referendum.
